Estera's mum Ela (left) died of stomach cancer in 2024

A close-up photograph in a hospital room showing Estera and Ela seated closely together for a selfie. Ela is wearing a light pink hospital robe and Estera wears a green jumper

I'm angry my Jehovah's Witness mum died - she didn't want to 'disobey God'

When Estera Pawlak's mother Ela was diagnosed with stomach cancer, she was offered potentially life-saving surgery to remove the tumour.

But the Jehovah's Witness refused as it could have involved a blood transfusion - a procedure that was forbidden in the religion until earlier this year.

Ela had chemotherapy in her native Poland but nothing could keep the disease at bay and she died in Aberdeen in 2024, aged 63.

Estera said the rule change on blood transfusions by the Jehovah's Witnesses made her angry.

"My mum could still be alive," she said. "They took her away from my siblings, my kids, my nieces and nephews.

"She missed out on so much of her life because of something that wasn't actually true."

Estera, now 30, was brought up as a Jehovah's Witness in Aberdeen but moved away from the religion as she grew older.

Her mum moved from Scotland to Świecie in Poland in December 2022 to look after her elderly mother and within months was diagnosed with stomach cancer.

She refused surgery and made inquiries with the religious organisation about alternative treatments - but Estera said she never got an answer.

In the meantime, the symptoms of the cancer began to take hold.

Ela got to meet her second born granddaughter but won't see her grow up

A close-up photograph of Ela sitting in a padded chair, holding her second granddaughter wrapped in a cream-coloured sleepsuit decorated with small bird illustrations.

Estera told BBC Scotland: "It should have just been an easy operation to remove part of her stomach.

"The Jehovah's Witness council gave her no plan to move forward, so my mum kept refusing care and became more and more unwell.

"I went to see her three months after the diagnosis and she was in a palliative care ward. It was crazy, I questioned, 'why are you here?'

"She was still so full of life and the most optimistic person you could ever meet. I couldn't understand that she was now dying."

Over the next 12 months, Ela had chemotherapy and medication to boost her red blood cells but it was not enough to keep the disease at bay.

"Even with the chemo and other medications we tried, we were back to square one - mum still needed the operation and a blood transfusion," Estera said.

"At this point it became heartbreaking. She was refusing care and the operation. It felt like mum was giving up, like we weren't good enough.

"But the way she explained it to us was choosing the operation would be like cheating on God. In her faith she felt like she had a relationship with him and couldn't let him down.

"Mum was terrified, she had so much life in her and she wanted to live, but she also said she wouldn't be able to live with herself if she disobeyed God."

Ela had 'so much life in her' according to her daughter

A portrait-style photograph taken in a hospital room showing Ela and her first born granddaughter seated closely together and looking toward the camera.

After a year of palliative care in Poland, Ela moved back to Scotland in January 2024.

Hours after landing she was rushed to hospital because her condition had deteriorated. She died 10 months later.

In March 2026, Jehovah's Witnesses updated their policy on blood transfusions to allow members to have their own blood removed, stored, and "given back" in medical procedures.

In September, they changed the policy to allow component transfusion. This allows the transfusion of plasma, red blood cells, and platelets.

The transfusion of whole blood is still not allowed.

When she learned about the change in rules, Estera said she had never felt anger like it. She thought it was insulting to everyone who had lost a loved one due to the rule in the past.

"I was in shock for a long time, I couldn't believe it was real. Then the anger came."

She added that thinking about the last months of her mother's life "just breaks me to pieces".

Estera was pregnant with her second daughter during the last year of her mum's life

Ela rests her hand on her daughter's baby bump. An intravenous cannula and medical tubing are attached to one hand, and a hospital identification wristband is visible. A printed ultrasound image rests on the patient's lap.

Dileep Lobo, a professor of gastrointestinal surgery at the University of Nottingham who has co-authored papers on treating Jehovah's Witness patients, said the blood policy update was a "game changer" and will save many lives.

"It will save a lot of lives and give us a lot more options for treating people," he said.

"A lot more operations will go ahead because of the rule change."

And he confirmed that without surgery to remove a tumour, treatment for stage two gastric cancer would become palliative.

"So, it may prolong life and improve the quality, but it isn't a cure and without the surgery ultimately the disease will progress and the patient dies," he said.

Andrew Basoo, the national spokesman for Jehovah's Witnesses, said the organisation was "saddened" when they heard someone had lost a loved one in death.

He said "They deserve to be heard respectfully and compassionately.

"Questions about their loved one's treatment warrant careful consideration of the medical evidence and that person's expressed wishes.
